name: Equol

lead: Equol is a compound formed when intestinal bacteria convert daidzein, a soy isoflavone. Only about 30 to 50 percent of people have bacteria that make it, so some people take it directly as a supplement.

Its appearance angle is skin and hormone-related. Topical equol has been linked to antioxidant and anti-aging claims, and animal studies suggest anti-androgenic effects that raise interest for hair and acne. Human trials focus on menopausal symptoms and bone turnover.

paras: It is used as an oral supplement (often S-equol) or in topical skincare, and is discussed alongside soy foods.
It acts on estrogen receptors, so hormone-sensitive conditions are a consideration. Reviews describe isoflavones as potential endocrine disruptors in some people as well as beneficial in others.

chain: Gut bacteria convert soy daidzein to equol
Estrogen receptor beta activity, antioxidant effects
angle.text: Equol is discussed for anti-aging skin effects and for possible anti-androgenic activity; human evidence centres on menopause.

lead: Equol is a nonsteroidal estrogen-like compound made from daidzein by gut bacteria; about 30 to 50 percent of people make it, with higher rates in East Asia than in Western countries.[1] S-equol binds preferentially to estrogen receptor beta.[1][2]

Topical equol has been reported to have antioxidant effects, and animal studies suggest anti-androgenic action, including reduced 5-alpha reductase and DHT, though the supporting skin data are limited or industry-linked.[1]
Human studies address menopausal symptoms and bone biomarkers rather than appearance directly.[3][4]

paras: S-equol preferentially binds estrogen receptor beta and may act like a selective estrogen receptor modulator; it is absorbed quickly with high bioavailability.[1] Gut microbiota determine whether people produce it.[2]

A systematic review of isoflavone supplements, including daidzein, genistein and S-equol, found reduced hot flashes beyond placebo and slower lumbar bone loss, with heterogeneous protocols.[3] A 12-month randomised trial of fermented soy containing equol with resveratrol reported improved bone turnover biomarkers in postmenopausal women.[4] No trials have tested equol for skin appearance or hair.
